589.s: Mendelsohn changed how he looked at music and life; as a teenager he was hurt that religious leaders did not speak up for school integration.
589.q: No. Prior to Dorothy Mendelsohn, I looked at things, either the physical aspect of it, materials, or mentally. Does it stimulate your mind? 104.t: Church of England religion in her childhood home

92.t: Church music, Methodist and Baptist, and a daughter who is a nun

566.s: The family lived next door to Ann Street Baptist Church, with Sunday School, the eleven o'clock service and the evening B.Y.P.U. taking up most of Sunday.
566.q: Yes, Ann Street Baptist Church. It's still, it's not in the same place but it's down the street. And we used to have to get up and go to Sunday School. Stayed for the morning service, you know.

566.t: Church music, Mahalia Jackson and not mixing gospel with club work
566.s: Humes dislikes modern church music that sounds like rock and roll. She admires Marion Williams and met Mahalia Jackson in Chicago around 1939-40, and does not think church songs belong in club work.
566.q: Because they play the church music and they dance and I don't know, there's something about it that I don't like to do church music like that.

418.t: Methodist upbringing and no funeral parades at home

125.t: Christian household radio, church choir exchanges and America

621.s: He says his family and most downtown musicians were Catholic.

1056.s: George took no interest in voodoo because his strict Catholic mother raised him in the church.

143.s: His mother played organ, taught him spirituals and black history, and he stopped attending church once he left.
143.q: All kind of music. My mother knew more music than anybody I ever met in my life. When I was a little kid, I was singing a lot of stuff that people started singing later on.

527.t: Church community, living in the parsonage, grandfather's death
527.s: Close-knit church-centred black community, living in the parsonage, grandfather's death, early lack of awareness of racism, Sunday church routine.
527.q: We lived in the parsonage. The parsonage is always next door to the church. We lived there until he died. After we had been out there for three or four years, he died.

144.t: Religions that are not inclusive; his wife's Catholicism
144.s: Fuller says religions bother him as exclusive, recalling the Jesuit school and his devout wife.
144.q: That’s why few religions bother me. They're not all inclusive. I always had this trouble in the Jesuit school. Everything I read from Job two ecclesiastical, it is not inclusive. There is nothing about the whole race of China. Which is a third of the world population. Ying and yang.

491.t: Baptist church, the organ and Miss Conley
491.s: Golson describes his Baptist background, being enthralled by the church organist, and hearing little of the sermon.
491.q: Yeah. We were Baptist background. My mother used to sing in the choir. Not the particular time when I was going to church, but when she met my father, that’s what she was doing. Yes, the thing that enthralled me was that organ that Miss Conley used to play. The sermon, what he was saying, went in…

224.t: His mother's Sanctified church and playing drums there
224.s: He attended his mother's Pentecostal church and played bass drum and cymbals at his uncle's church.
224.ch: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
224.q: The church was in our section of town then. Probably you’d see some white people come to there. Very few. I know there was an Italian guy called Brother Tony. I used to see him. He used to come with this bald head. He used to come there. He was Sanctified, because my mother went to a Sanctified…

135.t: Mother, Fat Mama, gospel singing and church life
135.s: Heath's mother sang in the choir, his Choctaw grandmother was devout, and he sang in a family gospel quartet and played violin; his father avoided church.
135.q: Mama was a choir singer in the 19th Street Baptist Church and her mother, my grandmother, who we used to call “Fat Mama,” it was Mama and Fat Mama, and it finally ended up being “Fatsie,” what a beautiful woman she was. She was part Choctaw.

451.s: Hall rejects belief in God after Jehovah's Witnesses and finds meaning in the moment.
451.q: (laughs) I’m sorry, I’m in a goofy state. As all relatively innocent little kids are, you, you kinda… somebody says, “Well, this is your religion,” and you go to church and this happened to Jesus and this and that… (laughs) And then, when my dad split, as I mentioned, my brother and I went to live…

111.t: Music at home and the Baptist church
111.s: His mother taught herself piano and spirituals; the family went to church, and his father was a deacon at Trinity Baptist.
111.q: Well not really. My mother taught herself, we had a piano, and she taught herself how to play church song. Old spirituals and things like that. They always sang in senior choir and we all went to Sunday school. We’d always run around to the big event of the week, which was going to church on…

492.t: Howlin' Wolf, the church and grandparents' spirituality
492.s: Lloyd calls Wolf the baddest cat, then describes the church his grandfather built, Pentecostal services that frightened him, and grandparents' heritage.
492.ch: Blues, church and the call to music
492.q: Look, that’s a very profound thing that you just touched upon about communication and Wolf and stuff. Howlin’ Wolf was the baddest cat that I ever played with on that circuit. On the blues cast - because you know, he’d [Imitates Howlin’ Wolf]...

686.s: His Catholic upbringing inspired the programmatic album using his band and his brothers' bands, which he compares to Ellington's approach.
686.q: Pontius Pilate’s Decision was a very important recording for me, based on a lot of the stories that I heard, growing up as a Catholic child. Every Sunday we’d hear these stories in church. They shaped my ideology and my philosophy about things that are important. I had the opportunity to record. So…

672.t: Baptist and Pentecostal church, and singing in the Methodist choir
672.s: Called a sinner by her step-family for singing secular songs, she sang in the Methodist choir by herself.
672.q: Yeah. When I was down in the country, I went to little one – little tiny, small church. That was Baptist. Then, when my father married Mom, she was Pentecostal. That was a whole other thing. At eight years old, to be a sinner was kind of hard to swallow, and I did not swallow it. I didn’t believe…

373.t: Black gospel and preachers versus klezmer; Daddy Grace in Harlem
373.s: He contrasts participatory black church music with klezmer, recalls gospel at WMEX and first visiting a Harlem church after coming to New York.
373.q: That is participatory music. One of the things I began to collect, still when I was a teenager, were recordings of black preachers and their congregations. That was – wow. At the radio station where I worked for quite a while – WMEX – on Saturday nights we had the local gospel guys coming in. That…

565.t: Church, marriage into Protestantism and belief
565.s: A short exchange on the church where he married and his view of belief.
565.q: Protestant. I was Catholic, but I married a Protestant. I don’t believe in the Protestant, this-and-that... It’s what you believe. The word is “believe.” If someone asked me, “Do you believe in God?” and I say, “No.” I say, “Do you believe in God?” He goes, “Yes.” To me, it means the same. We both…

509.t: How church music feels different from Debussy and Garner
509.s: She distinguishes the fluid lyricism of Debussy and Garner from the soulful foot-patting feel of Baptist church music.
509.q: Oh no, no, no, no. The lyricism I hear with Debussy and Earl Garner is so fluid, it flows together. Now, in the church it‘s different. I hear a difference. I hear a different feel, you know.

553.t: Embracing Islam through the Ahmadiyya Movement
553.s: Introduced to the Ahmadiyya Movement in Chicago by trumpeter Talib Dawud, he joins in 1948 and describes what it gave him.
553.q: Uh yeah. No, during this period, uh 1947, I was introduced by Islam when I was in Chicago. Um...I was playing at a place called the Boogie Woogie Inn on the West Side of Chicago, and trumpet player came in to sit in with us. His name was Talib Dawud. Uh...and uh for some reason he had a...some…

80.t: Neighbours mending a sick man's farm, with singing and food
80.s: He describes the church community who repaired fences, plowed and cooked for a sick neighbour, while he played hymns on trumpet.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: They used to get together and sing, as I told you they sing, and when I got -- and the main -- another thing I got out of this was you go to church and you hear people say be good to this one, and be good to the helpless person, blah, blah, [and round and round we go.] I saw that happen. I asked…

87.s: He describes opening Father Divine's meetings with hot songs and hymns while hired preachers did the preaching.
87.ch: Virginia school and first Washington bands
87.q: All we'd do was open up his set, you know, and play a few songs for him, you know, and get the people coming in, you know. Meeting them, spare a few hymns and let them come on in singing the hymns. That's all we did --

409.t: Sacred Concerts and Duke's religion; the number written for Cootie
409.s: Duke read the Bible many times; he wrote a Sacred Concert piece for Cootie after trying it out on piano.
409.q: It was a funny thing. First he was playing it on the piano. He wasn't playing it, he was just running it over. He called me down and said, "Hey, Coots, come

0.ch: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
0.q: That's his uncle. We made those records in 1926, first orthophonic recordings, electrical recordings. Tommy -- later on, around about the early '30's, about the middle '30's, he joined Father Divine's church.

381.t: His Catholic upbringing and the Garvey movement's American Catholic Church
381.s: He belonged to St. Peter's American Catholic Church, which his Haitian father joined through the Garvey movement.
381.ch: Childhood, drums and early church bands
381.q: But the reason why he left the Roman Catholic Church was because after he joined the Garvey movement, the Garvey movement had a church that they started of their own, and they made it the American Catholic Church, so that's how I became a member of that church.

452.t: His mother's prayer and a Baptist upbringing
452.s: His mother tells of praying for his recovery, and Cobb says he was raised strictly Baptist.
452.ch: First bands, illness and Houston life
452.q: I'm 59 until August the 10th and I'll be 60. Now Stanley, are you getting your mathematics together? I was born in 1918; August 10th.

234.t: Sister Rosetta Tharpe, the Golden Gate Quartet and gospel in popular music
234.s: Gil recalls Tharpe singing gospel in clubs, and says Ray Charles brought gospel into popular music.
234.ch: Miles Davis stories and what jazz means
234.q: ............ in the clubs. I imagine a lot of people put her down for that. She probably had trouble with old folks who thought that she shouldn't be doing that in clubs. She had a lot of hit records on Decca (popular tunes?) like popular gospel you know. But then it took a long time to finally…

71.t: Church life and his father's gospel quartet
71.s: Church was central socially; his mother led the choir, his father sang bass in a prize-winning quartet with Wild Bill Davis's father.
71.q: I don't really know. Unless it was, you see he used to sing in the choir as a bass singer and my dad was a, he was a church going man, and he was quite active in all the church, so both was my mother. Yes, my mother. They/were active, very active in musical work, church music.

386.t: Honey Grove, Texas, and the gospel music of his childhood church
386.s: Price confirms he was born in Honey Grove, names nearby towns, and describes the hymns, a cappella songs, tambourines and triangle he first heard.
386.q: Greenville...Paris...you know, in the eastern area you had Greenville, Paris and, if you went far enough, you'd go to Denison, up on the Red River Valley. I mean, the Red River... north of Honey Grove.

96.s: Returning to the blind singers, he and Johnston discuss how spirituals and gospel differ and both involve improvisation.
96.q: Well that's the greatest improvisation of jazz in the world, to me. That's basic, that's and I know when we heard, my brother and I heard these blind men down there on Lake and Polina Street, that that, we just flipped then.

170.t: Leaving the church and Reverend Turner's taste in music
170.s: Ware drifts out of the church as he plays with the older boys; Turner disapproves and steers him toward country music and white radio bands.
170.q: but by that time when I started with those older boys in the neighborhood, they come around and asked Ms. Turner could I go out with them, and I just kind of dropped out of the church. In fact, the church just seemed like it kind of disintegrated; I don't know what happened. But I didn't go back to…

427.t: His Baptist church and Geneva Hurris, later met in New Orleans
427.s: He names the church on Independence and Charlotte and the preacher's daughter who played piano, whom he met again at the Dew Drop Inn.
427.ch: Black and Tan and Kansas City nightlife
427.q: I went to the Baptist Church, Reverend Hurris's (?) church. It was on Independence Avenue and Charlotte, right down the street from my house. That's where we had a...his daughter played the piano. Later on, I met her in New Orleans. She was playin' and workin' in a nightclub.

73.t: Church singing, the ukulele and street-corner quartets
73.s: His mother sang in the AME choir; he played ukulele and sang baritone in a street-corner quartet.
73.q: Well, I used -- before I left -- I used to -- I think after I came back -- after I came back to -- say -- buried my brother and my mother more or less -- Well, my mother was in the church.

149.t: Church music at Enon Ridge Methodist Church
149.s: His family sang in the church; he began playing trumpet in the choir at about nine, though his grandfather doubted the horn belonged in church.
149.q: My grandfather, that's, he was in what they call like an amen corner. And my uncles and my aunts, they was in the church. And then I used to, after I got old enough, at least so I could have my horn, I could, I went down and I joined them.

115.t: Only child; father's failed trumpet and constant churchgoing
115.s: He was an only child; his father fooled with a trumpet, his mother learned piano later, and he went to church and Sunday school all the time.
115.ch: Childhood in Tyler, Beaumont and Houston
115.q: Oh, yes, I went in the morning, go to Sunday school, I'd come back and I'd go to church with my mother. And we'd go to church at night.

124.t: Clinton Utterbach's choir and later ministry
124.s: McRae calls Utterbach's choir sensational and perfectionist, and notes he is now a radio minister.
124.q: That's the same Clinton Utterbach because they had the choir. I think he went to join church world or something, and he's on the air. He sounds the same man. Clinton Utterbach. He's a minister now.

86.t: The aunt, church organ and religious upbringing
86.s: His aunt, a hymn organist, helped him; he played organ at funerals and Sunday school.
86.q: Yeah, they didn't have any kids of their own at all. And my mother's mother's sister, they were part-Indians from the Kentucky reservation.

7.t: 'Man's extremity is God's opportunity'; Hinton's grandmother's hymns
7.s: They talk about faith, Hinton's churchgoing grandmother who was a slave, and her singing 'Amazing Grace'.
7.q: Well, they say (I think it said in the Bible, too), "Man's extremity is God's opportunity." Like when a man gets so low he can't help himself. You know, the average guy don't believe in God, and he gets so low he can't help himself and he'll say, "God help me."

77.t: Detesting dressing up, avoiding church, listening to Sunday services
77.s: Having dressed up so much in show business she dislikes hats and church clothes, so she stays home and listens to religious radio on Sundays.
77.q: And then another thing, Chris, I had to dress up so much in show business. I had to spend so much money for clothes. And a lot of these girls that have these smart shops on Madison Avenue and in the different big stores, I got my clothes strictly from them. And then Patou dressed me in Paris, you…

171.t: Gus Johnson in the church choir and borrowing Ramey's car
171.s: Ramey and Gus sang in the Trinity A.M.E. choir before McShann, and Gus used his car.
171.q: Because Gus and I, before he left to go up to Omaha, I was going to Western University, and he was going to school over there at Sumner, and -- but we belonged

473.t: Henry Allen on trips; Sunday school keeps kids off the streets
473.s: Mrs. Allen stayed home to run Sunday school while her husband Henry went on trips; the Sunday school gave neglected kids somewhere to go, and Jones also went to church with his mother and grandmother.
473.ch: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
473.q: His name was Henry Allen. So he would usually go on the trips with us all the time, because she stayed there to keep that Sunday school going, if you were out of town. So that Sunday school still went on you know.

239.t: Danny Williams's parents and the Williams Singers
239.s: Jones knows only that the Williams Singers were famous spiritual singers who had broken up before he joined Danny.
239.ch: Follow-up questions, Bird and the Ellington sidemen
239.q: I didn't -- I never heard them. By the time I was with Danny, oh they had long broken up.
